text: Readout error mitigation corrects a known distortion in the measurement step. But what about error that accumulates during the circuit itself, from imperfect gates? You can't run a circuit with zero noise on real hardware to see what the ideal answer would have been — but you can estimate it, using zero-noise extrapolation.

You can never run your circuit at literally zero noise — it's a physical property of the device, not a dial you can turn down past its current setting. But you can deliberately run the same circuit with more noise than normal, in a controlled way. If you measure your result at a few different noise levels and the pattern is predictable, you can fit a curve through those points and extrapolate backward to zero noise, a point you never actually visited. The noise-scale factor, lambda, is 1 for normal, 2 for doubled, and so on.

The standard way to scale up noise without changing what the circuit ideally computes is gate folding: take a gate G and replace it with G, followed by its inverse, followed by G again. Mathematically that's exactly equivalent to G in the ideal case — the extra pair cancels out perfectly. But on real hardware, each of those three executions carries its own real error, so the effective error roughly triples, while the ideal computation stays completely unchanged.

Here's a deliberately simple teaching model where the noisy expectation value scales exactly linearly with lambda. At lambda 1, E is 0.72. At lambda 2, E is 0.64. A straight line through those two points, extrapolated back to lambda zero, is 2 times E of 1 minus E of 2, which works out to exactly 0.80 — the true ideal value, recovered exactly, because this teaching example was constructed to be exactly linear.

That linear relationship was built into the example on purpose, specifically so the arithmetic is fully checkable by hand. Real hardware noise scaling is often only approximately linear, and for larger lambda the real decay frequently looks closer to exponential. In practice, production tools more often use a Richardson extrapolation or an exponential fit, chosen based on how the measured data actually behaves.

You don't typically hand-roll gate folding and curve fitting. The mitiq library is a dedicated error-mitigation toolkit built to work directly with Qiskit circuits, implementing ZNE with a choice of folding strategies and extrapolation fits. On real IBM hardware, qiskit-ibm-runtime's EstimatorV2 primitive exposes a resilience_level option that can apply ZNE automatically, without you managing the folding and fitting steps yourself.
Chapter 7 closes with a lab that puts readout correction and zero-noise extrapolation to work together on the same numbers, so the connections between them stop being abstract.
